annotations.keyFindings: Holding HbA1c requests within 80 days cut early repeats from 17 to 6 percent over 12 months; 4.3 percent of holds were overridden; no important delay was found in 200 reviewed holds.
annotations.limitations: Uncontrolled before-and-after in one laboratory; safety review of 200 holds cannot exclude rare harm.

annotations.keyFindings: Three months was agreed as the HbA1c monitoring interval, with exceptions for pregnancy, suspected rapid change, new diagnosis and red cell turnover conditions; hold rules need a simple override and a harm review.
annotations.limitations: Consensus based; indirect evidence for most intervals.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 1,905 held requests, 11.1 percent were overridden, 58 percent of overrides for accepted exceptions; median time to override 1 working day.
39 percent of clinicians felt diabetes monitoring rules interfered with judgement; a one-sentence reason and a clear override route improved acceptance.
annotations.limitations: Survey response not reported; practices already using rules.

annotations.keyFindings: The 10 percent of practices with the most early repeats produced 38 percent of them, more often with pharmacist requesting and high locum use.
annotations.limitations: No individual clinical reasons; small follow-up for feedback.

claims.text: In a regional laboratory, a rule holding HbA1c requests made within 80 days reduced early repeat requests from 17 percent to 6 percent over 12 months.
claims.passage: Early repeat requests fell from 17 percent to 6 percent of HbA1c requests over 12 months.
claims.interpretation: A hold rule can work at scale; the size of change is a planning value only.

claims.text: A review of 200 held requests found no case in which the hold delayed a treatment decision judged important by two diabetologists.
claims.passage: A review of 200 held requests found no case in which the hold delayed a treatment decision judged important by two diabetologists.
claims.interpretation: Reassuring but too small to exclude rare harm; the pilot needs its own safety review.

claims.text: Under an interval rule in 18 practices, requesters overrode 11.1 percent of 1,905 held requests, 58 percent of overrides matched an accepted exception, and the median time from hold to override was 1 working day.
claims.passage: Requesters overrode 212 (11.1 percent); the reason matched an accepted exception in 58 percent of overrides
claims.interpretation: Gives planning values for override frequency and timeliness.

claims.text: In practices using hold rules, 39 percent of primary care clinicians felt that rules on diabetes monitoring interfered with their clinical judgement.
claims.passage: 39 percent felt that rules on diabetes monitoring interfered with their clinical judgement
claims.interpretation: Acceptability is a real risk and must be measured, with comment wording tested.

claims.text: A consensus statement agreed three months as the HbA1c monitoring interval with exceptions for pregnancy, suspected rapid change, new diagnosis and conditions affecting red cell turnover.
claims.passage: For HbA1c, three months was agreed for monitoring established diabetes, with exceptions for pregnancy, suspected rapid change, new diagnosis and conditions affecting red cell turnover.
claims.interpretation: Defines the override categories the safety review should test.

synthesis: Five retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A hold rule cut early repeat HbA1c requests from 17 to 6 percent in one laboratory without important delays in 200 reviewed holds, and override analyses elsewhere give planning values (about 11 percent overridden, median 1 working day). A consensus statement defines exceptions and asks for harm review. Acceptability is uncertain: 39 percent of clinicians felt diabetes monitoring rules interfered with judgement. Early repeats concentrate in a minority of practices. The evidence supports a small pilot with explicit progression criteria and a safety review, not immediate rollout.
gradeRationale: Uncontrolled evaluations, a consensus statement and a survey; consistent but indirect for these practices, and too small to exclude rare harm.
summary: Five records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.
